65.title: The Execution
paragraphs: It was near midnight. The moon, notched by its waning and stained red by the last of the storm, was rising behind the little town of Armentières, which stood out against that sickly light as a dark outline of rooftops and the open skeleton of its high steeple. Opposite, the Lys rolled its waters like a river of molten tin, while on the far bank the black mass of the trees showed against a stormy sky overrun with heavy copper clouds, making a kind of dusk in the middle of the night. To the left rose an old abandoned mill with motionless sails, and in its ruins an owl repeated its cry, shrill and monotonous and exactly timed. Here and there across the plain, to the right and left of the road the grim procession followed, stood a few low squat trees, like misshapen dwarves crouched to watch for men at that sinister hour.

From time to time a broad flash of lightning opened the horizon along its whole width, snaked above the black mass of the trees, and came down like a terrible scimitar to cut the sky and the water in two. Not a breath of wind moved in the heavy air. A deathly silence lay on everything; the ground was wet and slick with the rain that had just fallen, and the revived grass gave up its scent more strongly.
Two servants dragged Milady along, each holding her by an arm. The executioner walked behind, and behind him came Lord de Winter, d'Artagnan, Athos, Porthos and Aramis.
Planchet and Bazin came last.
The two servants were leading Milady towards the river. Her mouth was silent, but her eyes spoke with their own unsayable eloquence, appealing in turn to each man she looked at.
Finding herself a few steps ahead of the others, she said to the servants:
"A thousand pistoles to each of you if you help me escape. But if you hand me over to your masters, I have avengers close by who will make you pay dearly for my death."
Grimaud hesitated. Mousqueton shook in every limb.
Athos, who had heard Milady's voice, came quickly forward, and Lord de Winter did the same.
"Send these servants away," he said. "She has spoken to them. They are no longer to be trusted."
Planchet and Bazin were called, and took the places of Grimaud and Mousqueton.
At the water's edge the executioner came up to Milady and bound her hands and feet.
Then she broke her silence to cry out:
"You are cowards. You are miserable murderers. It takes ten of you to cut one woman's throat. Take care — if nobody comes to save me, I shall be avenged."
"You are not a woman," said Athos coldly. "You do not belong to the human race. You are a demon escaped from hell, and we are going to send you back to it."
"Ah, you virtuous gentlemen!" said Milady. "Bear in mind that whoever lays a finger on my head is a murderer in his turn."

"An executioner may kill and be no murderer for it, madame," said the man in the red cloak, striking the flat of his broad sword. "He is the last judge, that is all. Nachrichter, as our German neighbours say."
And as he bound her while he spoke, Milady let out two or three savage cries, which had a strange and sombre effect flying off into the night and losing themselves in the depths of the wood.
"But if I am guilty, if I have committed the crimes you accuse me of," she screamed, "take me before a court. You are not judges, that you may sentence me."
"I offered you Tyburn," said Lord de Winter. "Why would you not take it?"
"Because I do not want to die!" cried Milady, struggling. "Because I am too young to die!"
"The woman you poisoned at Béthune was younger than you, madame, and she is dead," said d'Artagnan.
"I will go into a convent. I will become a nun," said Milady.
"You were in a convent," said the executioner, "and you left it to ruin my brother."
Milady gave a cry of terror and dropped to her knees.
The executioner lifted her under the arms and made to carry her towards the boat.
"Oh, my God!" she cried. "My God! Are you going to drown me?"

There was something so tearing in those cries that d'Artagnan, who of them all had hunted Milady hardest, let himself down onto a stump and bowed his head, stopping his ears with the palms of his hands. Even so he could still hear her threatening and crying out.
D'Artagnan was the youngest of all these men, and his heart failed him.
"Oh, I cannot watch this horrible thing! I cannot agree to this woman dying like this!"
Milady had caught those few words, and had seized on a glimmer of hope.
"D'Artagnan! D'Artagnan!" she cried. "Remember that I loved you!"
The young man got to his feet and took a step towards her.
But Athos drew his sword at once and stood in his way.
"If you take one step more, d'Artagnan," he said, "you and I shall cross blades."
D'Artagnan fell to his knees and prayed.
"Come," Athos went on. "Executioner, do your duty."
"Willingly, my lord," said the executioner, "for as surely as I am a good Catholic, I firmly believe I am doing right in carrying out my office upon this woman."
"Very well."
Athos took a step towards Milady.

"I forgive you," he said, "the harm you have done me. I forgive you my broken future, my lost honour, my defiled love, and my salvation put in danger for ever by the despair you threw me into. Die in peace."
Lord de Winter came forward in his turn.
"I forgive you," he said, "the poisoning of my brother and the murder of His Grace Lord Buckingham. I forgive you the death of poor Felton, and I forgive you your attempts upon myself. Die in peace."

"And I," said d'Artagnan, "ask you to forgive me, madame, for having provoked your anger by a trick unworthy of a gentleman. In exchange I forgive you the murder of my poor love, and your cruelties towards me. I forgive you, and I weep for you. Die in peace."
"I am lost," murmured Milady in English. "I must die."
Then she rose to her feet unaided and cast about her one of those clear looks that seemed to leap from an eye of flame.
She saw nothing.
She listened, and heard nothing.
She had none but enemies around her.
"Where am I to die?" she said.
"On the other bank," answered the executioner.
Then he put her into the boat, and as he was setting foot in it himself to follow her, Athos handed him a sum of money.
"Here," he said. "This is the price of the execution. Let it be plain that we are acting as judges."
"Very well," said the executioner. "And now let this woman know in her turn that I am not plying my trade, but doing my duty."
And he threw the money into the river.
The boat drew away towards the left bank of the Lys, carrying the guilty woman and her executioner. All the rest stayed on the right bank, where they had fallen to their knees.
The boat slid slowly along the ferry rope, beneath the reflection of a pale cloud that hung over the water at that moment.
They saw it touch the far bank; the figures stood out black against the reddish horizon.
During the crossing Milady had managed to work loose the cord binding her feet. On reaching the shore she sprang lightly to the ground and ran.
But the earth was wet. At the top of the slope she slipped and fell on her knees.
Some superstitious thought must have struck her. She understood that Heaven was refusing her its help, and she stayed as she was, head bowed and hands clasped.

Then from the other bank they saw the executioner slowly raise both his arms; a ray of moonlight caught the blade of his broad sword; the two arms came down; they heard the hiss of the blade and the victim's cry, and then a shortened mass sank under the blow.

The executioner then unfastened his red cloak, spread it on the ground, laid the body on it, threw the head after it, knotted it by the four corners, hoisted it onto his shoulder and stepped back into the boat.
Reaching the middle of the Lys he stopped the boat, and holding his burden out over the river he called aloud:
"Let the justice of God be done!"
And he let the body fall into the deepest part of the water, which closed over it.
Three days later the four musketeers were back in Paris. They had kept within the limits of their leave, and that same evening they paid their usual call on Monsieur de Tréville.
"Well, gentlemen," the good captain asked them, "did you enjoy yourselves on your excursion?"
"Prodigiously," answered Athos through his teeth.
